title: YOU CALL IT A BLESSING. BUT HAS HAVING MORE MADE YOU MORE GENEROUS—OR JUST MORE COMFORTABLE?
paragraphs: YOU CALL IT A BLESSING. BUT HAS HAVING MORE MADE YOU MORE GENEROUS—OR JUST MORE COMFORTABLE?
Maybe the most dangerous thing about having more is not that you have it. It is that, somewhere along the way, you may stop asking why God allowed it into your hands.
There is a prayer almost nobody posts after the promotion comes through.
Nobody frames it beside the photograph of the new house.
Nobody writes it beneath the picture of the new car, the successful business, the full table, the growing bank account, or the vacation they once could only dream about.
We usually say something simpler.
“God blessed me.”
And perhaps He did.

Scripture certainly does not teach that possessing material things is automatically sinful. Abraham possessed great wealth. Job had enormous possessions, lost them, and later received abundance again. Wealthy people such as Joseph of Arimathea used what they had in ways connected with honoring Christ.
The problem is not automatically what is sitting in your garage.
The problem is what may be sitting on the throne of your heart.
Because there is another question that should follow the words “God blessed me.”
What is this blessing producing in me?
Has having more made you more generous?
More grateful?
More compassionate?
More available to God?
More willing to quietly meet someone else's need?
Or has having more simply made it possible to build a more comfortable version of the same self-centered life?
That question hurts.
It hurts because comfortable materialism rarely announces itself as idolatry.
It looks respectable.
It pays the bills.
It works hard.
It may attend church.
It may thank God before dinner.
It may even post Bible verses beside photographs of things it has purchased.
And yet Jesus warned that a human life cannot be measured by the abundance of possessions.
Paul later gave Timothy instructions that should make every Christian who has been entrusted with material resources stop for a moment.

“Charge them that are rich in this world, that they be not highminded, nor trust in uncertain riches, but in the living God, who giveth us richly all things to enjoy; That they do good, that they be rich in good works, ready to distribute, willing to communicate; Laying up in store for themselves a good foundation against the time to come, that they may lay hold on eternal life.”
—1 Timothy 6:17–19, KJV
Listen to the tension in that passage.
Paul does not tell Timothy that Christians who possess wealth must hate everything they own.
He does not say that enjoying God's provision is inherently evil.
He says God “giveth us richly all things to enjoy.”
But in the same breath, he destroys the illusion that possessions were given merely so that the person possessing them could become increasingly absorbed with themselves.
The Greek becomes especially striking.
Paul tells the wealthy:
ἀγαθοεργεῖν, πλουτεῖν ἐν ἔργοις καλοῖς, εὐμεταδότους εἶναι, κοινωνικούς
agathoergein, ploutein en ergois kalois, eumetadotous einai, koinōnikous.
In context, the sense is that they are to do good, to be rich in good works, to be generous and willing to share.
Notice the reversal.
Paul does not merely ask, “How rich are you?”
He asks what you are rich in.
There is a kind of poverty that can live inside an expensive house.
A person can have overflowing closets and an empty generosity.
A person can upgrade everything except their compassion.
A person can increase their income while decreasing their dependence on God.
A person can become richer every year and somehow have less room in their heart for the suffering person standing beside them.
And perhaps the most frightening part is that they can call the entire process “blessing.”
Imagine standing before Jesus with everything you once prayed for.
The house.
The savings.
The business.
The wardrobe.
The gadgets.
The investments.
The things you bought because you had finally “made it.”
Now imagine Him asking:
“What did having more make you become?”
Not because salvation can be purchased with generosity.
It cannot.
Not because Christians earn heaven by giving money away.
They do not.
We are saved by grace through faith, not by works, so that no one may boast.
But the grace that saves us does not leave the heart untouched.
Jesus does not merely rewrite our eternal destination.
He begins rewriting what we love.
And that includes what we do with what we possess.
There was another man in Scripture who had more.
Jesus told his story in Luke 12.
His land produced abundantly.
That is important.
The harvest itself was not presented as theft.
The man had a genuine abundance problem.
His barns were too small.
So he began talking to himself.
“What shall I do?”
“I will do this.”
“I will pull down my barns.”
“I will build greater.”
“I will bestow all my fruits and my goods.”
“My soul...”
“My goods...”
“My barns...”
“My future...”
His world had become astonishingly small.
There was enough food for many people, but apparently only one person existed in his imagination.
Himself.
Then he told his soul that it had plenty stored for many years.
Relax.
Eat.
Drink.
Be merry.
Comfort had finally arrived.
But eternity interrupted his retirement plan.
God called him a fool.
Not because barns are sinful.
Not because planning is sinful.
Not because having a successful harvest is sinful.
Jesus exposes something deeper.
The man had accumulated treasure for himself while remaining poor toward God.
He had abundance without eternal perspective.
Provision without stewardship.
Resources without generosity.
Full barns.
Empty hands.
And before another sunrise could validate his plans, his life was required of him.
That story is uncomfortable because modern barns have become beautiful.
Sometimes we call them portfolios.
Closets.
Garages.
Storage rooms.
Second properties.
Online carts.
Upgrade cycles.
Lifestyle goals.
None of those things is automatically sinful.
That is precisely why this requires discernment rather than simplistic condemnation.
The question is not merely, “Do I own something expensive?”
The deeper question is:
Does something expensive own me?
Could God interrupt your plans?
Could generosity inconvenience you?
Could another person's need change what you intended to buy?
Could you give without needing applause?
Could you help somebody who can never repay you?
Could you live below what you technically could afford because the kingdom of God matters more than displaying everything you can acquire?
Could you lose something and still worship?
That last question exposes us.
Because sometimes we discover whether something was a gift or a god only when it is taken away.
We say, “God gave this to me.”
Then we clutch it as though He has no right to touch it again.
We say, “Everything belongs to God.”
Until obedience becomes expensive.
We sing, “I surrender all.”
Then quietly add:
“Except my lifestyle.”
Jesus said something devastatingly simple:
“For where your treasure is, there will your heart be also.”
—Matthew 6:21, KJV
He did not say your treasure merely reveals something about your heart.
His words are even more penetrating.
Your heart follows treasure.
That means spending is never merely financial.
It can become spiritual formation.
Every repeated decision whispers something into the soul.
More for me.
More for me.
More for me.
Until “enough” becomes a destination permanently moving away from us.
The salary you once prayed for becomes the salary you now complain about.
The house you once would have wept to own becomes the house that suddenly needs renovating because someone else has something newer.
The phone that amazed you two years ago becomes embarrassing.
The clothes that once felt luxurious become ordinary.
Comfort has an appetite.
Feed it without restraint and it rarely says, “Thank you. That is enough.”
It usually learns a new word.
More.
And this is where the Gospel confronts us—not with shame designed to destroy us, but with grace powerful enough to free us.
Look at Jesus.
The center of Christianity is not a God demanding that poor humans make Him richer.
The center of Christianity is the Son of God giving Himself for sinners who could never repay Him.
Paul writes of Christ:
—2 Corinthians 8:9, KJV
In context, Paul is encouraging Christian generosity, and he anchors that generosity in Christ Himself.
That changes everything.
Christian giving is not fundamentally, “Give enough and maybe God will love you.”
It is:
Look at how you have already been loved.
Jesus did not purchase your redemption with spare change.
He gave Himself.
The cross was not divine leftovers.
Christ did not rescue us because we deserved investment.
We brought Him sin.
He brought us mercy.
We brought rebellion.
He brought reconciliation.
We brought guilt.
He brought His blood.
We brought a debt we could never pay.
He brought grace we could never earn.
That is the scandal.
And then comes grace.
The greedy can become generous.
The materialistic can become kingdom-minded.
The person who spent decades building monuments to themselves can begin using what remains of their life to serve others.
The person whose identity was wrapped around possessions can discover an identity that thieves cannot steal, markets cannot crash, rust cannot destroy, and death cannot confiscate.
Because Jesus rewrites everything.
Maybe this article is making you uncomfortable.
Good questions sometimes do.
But do not confuse conviction with condemnation.
The Gospel is not telling you to purchase forgiveness.
Christ already paid the price sinners could never pay.
The Gospel is calling you to repent, believe, and surrender.
Maybe you have spent years asking God for more while rarely asking Him what He wants you to do with what is already in your hands.
Maybe your prayer has been:
“Lord, increase me.”
Perhaps tonight it needs to become:
“Lord, search me.”
Search the way I spend.
Search the way I save.
Search what I envy.
Search what I display.
Search what I refuse to release.
Search the things I call necessities.
Search my excuses.
Search my fear of not having enough.
Search my desire to be seen as successful.
Search whether my possessions are serving Your kingdom—or whether I have slowly become their servant.
And Jesus, if I have mistaken comfort for Your approval, correct me.
If I have called greed ambition, expose it.
If I have called comparison motivation, expose it.
If I have called excess blessing while ignoring the opportunity to bless others, expose it.
Then forgive me.
Change me.
Teach me generosity that does not need cameras.
Teach me stewardship that remembers eternity.
Teach me to enjoy Your gifts without worshiping them.
Teach me to hold possessions with open hands because my life is already held securely in Yours.
That is a dangerous prayer.
Because God may not merely change your budget.
He may change your definition of wealth.
You may begin discovering that some of the richest moments of your life happen when nobody knows what you gave.
When a hungry person eats.
When a struggling family breathes again.
When a missionary receives support.
When Scripture reaches somebody searching for truth.
When a believer gets the discipleship resource they desperately needed.
When someone encounters the Gospel because another Christian decided the kingdom mattered more than keeping everything for themselves.
And before this becomes another emotional article you agree with and forget tomorrow, ask yourself one question:
What will change because I read this?
Not what did I feel.
What will change?
Maybe there is something you need to give.
Someone you need to help.
A purchase you need to reconsider.
A habit you need to confront.
A hidden idol you need to confess.
Or perhaps you simply need to stop measuring God's goodness by how many things He allows you to accumulate.
If this exposed something in you, do not hide behind religious language.
Not as a performance.
As honesty.
Someone reading those words may realize they are not the only believer wrestling with this.
Not because you need another saved post buried in a folder, but because comfort has a short memory. Return to 1 Timothy 6:17–19 when “more” starts whispering again.
Not to shame wealthy people.
Not to condemn people for owning things.
Send it privately to the person who has been wrestling with money, ambition, generosity, success, or contentment.
And if Gospel Warrior has been helping you return to Scripture, think more seriously about Christ, confront hidden compromise, heal through biblical truth, and grow deeper in the Gospel, stay close.
God's grace cannot be bought.
Because perhaps one of the greatest tests of abundance is not whether you thanked God when you received more.
It is whether receiving more made you look more like Jesus.
One day, every house belongs to somebody else.
Every car stops running.
Every device becomes obsolete.
Every fashionable thing becomes old.
Every account we controlled passes beyond our control.
Every possession eventually slips from our hands.
But what Christ has done in a surrendered life reaches beyond the grave.
So enjoy what God gives you with gratitude.
Provide responsibly for those entrusted to you.
Save wisely.
Work diligently.
Do not manufacture guilt where Scripture does not.
But never confuse having more with being more blessed spiritually.
Never let God's gifts become competitors for God's throne.
Never allow comfort to convince you that you have arrived.
And never forget that the greatest treasure Christianity offers was never something God placed inside your hands.
It was Someone who allowed His own hands to be pierced for you.
Maybe the question was never how much God placed in your hands—but whether, after receiving it, your hands still looked like His: open.
